Take-Home Exercise 1 - Geospatial Analytics for Public Good

Author

Kalpit Kulshrestha

Published

September 16, 2025

Modified

October 27, 2025

Objectives

In this take-home exercise, we are interested to investigate the spatial and spatio-temporal patterns of new businesses and firms established in Singapore for the first six months of 2025

The specific objectives of this take-home exercise are as follows:

  • To identify the “where” and “when” of new business entities, revealing clusters, patterns, and trends that are crucial for informed urban planning, resource allocation, and economic development.
  • To identify complex interaction patterns and emergent phenomena in the distribution of new businesses beyond simple proximity or density, such as clustering of related businesses, the influence of past trends on future locations, and the overall structural development of commercial areas, which are crucial for scientific urban planning and policy-making.

Assignment Task

Reference to: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Good

The Data

The following three dataset will be used in this exercise.which is accesed form the Infomration on Corporate Entities dataset of ACRA which has 27 CSV file for that refer here SSIC: Singapore Standard Industrial Classification

  1. Section-E : Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities.
  2. Section-G : Wholesale and retail trade
  3. Section-H : Transportation and storage

Installing the packages into R environment

Package Purpose
sf Provides a modern way to store, manipulate, and analyze spatial vector data (points, lines, polygons). Ideal for reading shapefiles and linking spatial attributes to your assignment data.
tmap Creates professional-looking thematic maps, both static and interactive. Useful for visualizing spatial patterns (e.g., hotspots, clusters) from your assignment dataset
tidyverse A collection of core data-wrangling and visualization packages (dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr, readr). Essential for cleaning, transforming, and plotting your assignment data before/after spatial analysis
rvest A web-scraping package to extract data from websites (tables, text, attributes). Handy if your assignment requires fetching external data like location details, business lists, or geo-coordinates
terra Handles raster data (e.g., satellite images, elevation models) efficiently. Useful when your assignment involves environmental layers, raster overlays, or extracting values at point locations.
spatstat A powerful framework for spatial point pattern analysis—testing clustering, dispersion, intensity, and spatial statistics. Helps if you’re analyzing where events or businesses occur
sparr Focuses on spatial and spatio-temporal kernel density estimation and risk analysis. Excellent for identifying hotspots and spatial risk zones in your assignment
spdep Provides tools for spatial dependence, weights matrices, and spatial regression models. Useful if your assignment involves testing spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I, LISA) or spatial lag/error models 
pacman::p_load(sf,tmap, tidyverse, rvest, terra, spatstat, sparr, spdep)

Reproducibilty

For reproducible results of this exercise, we will use seed value, 1234.

set.seed(1234)

Extracting Selected Business

section_E$registration_incorporation_date <- as.Date(section_E$registration_incorporation_date, format="%Y-%m-%d")

end_date <- as.Date("2025-06-30")
